executive_summary: AUD/JPY stood at 109.81 (payload spot 109.80799) on 2026-10-02, one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date. One Australian dollar buys 109.81 yen, and a rising pair means AUD is strengthening against JPY. The pair is down 2.13% over one month, 2.25% over three months and 2.50% over six, but still up 11.52% over twelve. It sits at the 71st percentile of its 52-week closing range, about 4.5% below the 28 August intraday high of 114.96. Spot is below the 50-day (112.08), 100-day (112.61) and 200-day (111.43) simple averages, yet 10.5% above a 200-week average (99.36) that is still rising. The story for this pair is a carry trade being repriced from the funding side. The 335bp RBA–BoJ policy gap is the widest in G10+SGD. Against it, the BoJ has hiked twice in 2026 and says more is coming, while the RBA at 4.60% is near the top of a cycle that its own labour market is starting to push back on. Three things matter for this pair that neither single-currency dossier shows on its own: speculators are crowded short the cross on both legs (legacy AUD net −46,814 contracts; JPY net +72.0K); Australia runs a US$29.0bn goods surplus with Japan, mostly energy; and the two legs' real exchange rates sit 50 points apart (BIS REER 116.11 vs 66.02). The settled verdict is tactically Bullish at conviction 2 (score +0.1978) and strategically Bearish at conviction 3 (score −0.3413). We express it in two steps: first, a short, catalyst-dependent long from 109.20–109.80, targeting 111.00–111.43 into the 28 October CPI / 30 October BoJ / 3 November RBA cluster, with a stop at 108.40; second, a strategic short re-established in that same 111.00–111.45 zone once the cluster has passed, with a 105.00 base-case target by end-March 2027. The main caveat is that the chart argues against the tactical leg: the pair has made lower highs and lower lows since late August and has broken below the post-intervention August low. Commentary published after the spot date also says November RBA hike bets have faded, which hits the main pillar of the tactical thesis. We therefore size the tactical long at half weight; the scored verdict stands as issued.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On valuation the two legs are the furthest apart of any pair in the benchmarking set. The BIS real effective exchange rate is 116.11 for AUD (the dearest in G10+SGD, +9.97% year-on-year) and 66.02 for JPY (the cheapest by 28.8 points, −6.50 year-on-year), a 50-point gap. The base dossier's World Bank PPP conversion factors put AUD/JPY fair value at 69.40, about 58% below spot. The quote dossier's REER-derived estimate puts it near 84, about 31% below spot. Both are dominated by Balassa-Samuelson price-level effects and neither is a timing signal. What is priced in at 109.81 is the 335bp carry and the expectation that it holds. What is not priced is any real-exchange-rate correction from a configuration in which Australia's real appreciation came while iron ore, 35% of its export revenue, fell 7.14%. Valuation is a strategic tailwind for a bearish view and irrelevant over four weeks. market_context.recent_regime: AUD/JPY spent April to August in a 111–115 distribution range. It topped at 114.96 on 28 August as the yen hit its intervention-era lows and the RBA-BoJ gap was at its widest. September broke the range: the quote leg rallied against every G10 currency as a 212.6K-contract speculative flip and the BoJ's 18 September hike repriced what yen funding costs. As one desk put it, this was a repricing of what yen funding will cost, not a liquidation of what it funds. The base leg gave no offset, because the RBA's 29 September hike landed alongside a US 10-year at the top of its range and a high-yield market 42bp wider on the month. The pair now sits just above its six-month low, crowded short on both legs, two weeks before the most consequential event cluster of the quarter.

Carry ranks the pair but does not drive it: September proved this, with a 2.13% one-month fall erasing about seven and a half months of carry. One desk framed AUD/JPY as offering about three and a half yen a year in carry against a fall of roughly five yen from near 115 since August. A bullish view is paid to wait; a bearish view pays about 352bp a year (about 193 pips over six months) to be held.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is +335bp: the RBA Cash Rate Target at 4.60% after a unanimous 25bp hike on 29 September against a BoJ overnight call rate target of 1.25% after a 7-2 hike on 18 September. That is the widest policy gap available in the benchmarking set and the single largest fundamental support under the pair. The gated payload carries a 10-year differential of +207.5bp on August monthly vintages; the two dossiers' live late-September cross-sections put it nearer +232bp (Australia 5.38%, Japan 3.06%), and the direction of travel there is compression, because the JGB 10-year has risen 141bp over a year while the Australian long end has been dragged along by a US selloff rather than by domestic repricing. The trajectory is the problem for the level: the RBA is at or near the top of its cycle with only 20% priced for 3 November, while the BoJ is early in a normalisation it has explicitly said will continue, with 25-38% priced for 30 October. Both legs therefore carry an underpriced hawkish option inside the same four-week window, which is why the net is Neutral rather than directional. The transmission is carry: 335bp annualised on a 109.808 spot accrues roughly 0.84% a month, and the listed-futures roll pays -351.9bp annualised, so a rolled long is paid about 3.5% a year — material as a ranking signal, immaterial against a cross whose 60-day realised volatility is 7.82%.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the first derivative of the differential matters more than its level, and it points one way: narrower. The gated calendar gives the BoJ three decisions inside the window — 30 October and 22 January, both carrying an Outlook Report projection round, plus 18 December — against two RBA decisions, 3 November and 8 December. The BoJ is 1.25% below a 2% target it has stated it intends to reach gradually, while the RBA sits 60bp above the top of its own band with unemployment at a post-COVID high of 4.6% and NAB business conditions negative for the first time since September 2020. Two BoJ hikes against at most one RBA hike takes the gap from 335bp toward 285-310bp, and the terminal-rate repricing that accompanies it is worth more than the delivered steps: the market carries roughly two BoJ hikes over twelve months where the quote dossier expects two inside six. The long end is already doing the work independently — the JGB 10-year now trades above the German Bund and 259bp above the Swiss Confederation, so Japan has stopped being the world's lowest-yielding major sovereign, which is a structural change to the funding-currency proposition rather than a cyclical one. The offset, and the reason confidence is 55 rather than higher, is that 335bp is a large cushion: the pair must fall roughly 1.7% over six months before a long is losing money against the forward.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Adjusted from default 0.18 / 0.10: -0.03 tactical and -0.02 strategic. The bilateral inflation gap is wide and has been stable for months, and the pair's sensitivity to data surprises runs disproportionately through the risk channel rather than the relative-data channel — AUD/JPY reacts more to a credit-spread move than to either country's CPI. tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is wide and widening at the headline. Australia's monthly CPI indicator re-accelerated to 4.0% year-on-year in August from 3.5% in July with trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% for a third month, while Japan's August core ex fresh food eased to 1.7%, a seventh consecutive month below target. That is a 190bp core gap in Australia's favour and the direction of travel is diverging further. Growth is also in Australia's favour on level: 2.14% year-on-year against Japan's 0.73%, the lowest in the benchmarking set. The asymmetry of the release calendar matters for the pair specifically: the Australian September quarter CPI on 28 October is a single quarterly print that compresses three months of expectation into one number five days before an RBA decision the market prices at 20%, whereas Japan's monthly series is already decelerating and its surprise potential is suppressed by government energy subsidies that cut the electricity component 2.4% year-on-year. Transmission to the pair is through the relative policy response: a trimmed mean at or above 3.7% moves 3 November pricing through 50% and lifts AUD/JPY directly, while a Japanese core print in line does nothing. The confidence of 52 is deliberately low because the Australian growth side is cracking — unemployment 4.6%, composite PMI 50.8, manufacturing 49.3 — and because the August Australian headline rests on a calendar event store rather than a published ABS page.

tactical.what_is_priced: Consensus treats the Australian trimmed mean as having plateaued at 3.6% and the Japanese core deceleration as extrapolable. The asymmetry is that only one of those two beliefs faces a high-impact quarterly test inside the window.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two inflation processes converge from opposite directions and the growth differential reverses sign in importance. Australia's shock is cost-push and is already destroying demand: NAB sales margins at -20 are the lowest since June 2020 with purchase costs rising 1.2% a quarter against final prices of 0.5%, real wages have fallen for a third consecutive quarter on a Wage Price Index of 3.2%, and business conditions are negative for the first time since September 2020. Japan's measured core is suppressed rather than absent: a producer price index of 7.6% sits above a consumer core of 1.7%, a 5.7-point unpassed pipeline, and the electricity component is being held down by a subsidy programme with an expiry date, while Shunto settled at 5.01% for a fourth consecutive year and Tankan three-year-ahead corporate inflation expectations sit at 2.6%, above target. The likely path is therefore Australian core decelerating toward the band while Japanese core re-accelerates toward and through 2%, narrowing a 190bp gap that is the fundamental justification for a 335bp policy gap. Transmission to the pair is through the relative reaction functions: converging inflation forces the RBA toward a pivot it is already being invited to make and gives the BoJ the cover it needs to keep going. Confidence is 55 rather than higher because Japanese private consumption contributed exactly zero to Q2 GDP and household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year, which is a real constraint on how far the Japanese side of the convergence can run.

factors.horizon_split: The horizons flip sign because the same energy shock does opposite things on different clocks. Over four weeks higher Australian inflation means a higher probability of an Australian hike, which lifts the pair. Over six months that inflation is compressing Australian margins and employment while the Japanese pipeline passes through, so the inflation gap that justifies the rate gap narrows from both ends. The inflection is the pair of October prints: the Australian September quarter CPI on 28 October and the Japanese October national CPI in the third week of November. Pass-2 addendum (post-spot information, not used to re-score): data released after the spot date chips at the tactical leg. The Melbourne Institute inflation gauge slowed from 0.5% to 0.3% month-on-month in September and ANZ job advertisements fell from 2.6% to 2.2%, and bets on a November RBA hike were reported to have fallen sharply. These are signpost readings against the tactical thesis, recorded in the Signposts section.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: AUD/JPY is the maximum-beta expression of global risk appetite in G10 FX: the base leg is the highest-beta commodity currency and the quote leg is the currency with the strongest negative VIX correlation, amplified because carry traders are structurally short it. The current cross-asset configuration is benign in level: VIX closed 16.07 at the 28th percentile of its one-year range, the S&P 500 is up 14.02% over twelve months and only 0.44% lower on the month, and US investment-grade spreads at 83bp are historically tight. For a pair whose entire transmission is risk beta, a low-volatility tape with equities intact is directly supportive. Two things keep confidence at 48. First, the deterioration is real at the margin: high-yield widened 42bp over the month to 302bp, the 83rd percentile of its one-year range, while investment grade held — the textbook early signature of risk appetite cracking at the low-quality end, and high yield is the series this pair tracks most closely. Second, the September move in global markets was made in rates rather than equities, with the US 10-year up 51bp to 5.24% at the 100th percentile of its one-year range, and a rates-driven risk event is the configuration in which the base leg underperforms its own carry. The net over four weeks is a supportive level with a deteriorating margin, which is a low-confidence Bullish rather than anything stronger.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor for this pair is an asymmetry argument and the asymmetry runs against it. VIX at 16.07 and investment grade at 83bp are near the floor of their post-crisis ranges: the distribution of six-month changes from such a starting point is heavily skewed to widening, and AUD/JPY is the single highest-beta G10 instrument to that widening because both legs move the same way. A credit-led risk event hits the base leg through commodity demand and the global growth channel and simultaneously bids the quote leg through repatriation of roughly 3.5 trillion dollars of Japanese foreign securities and through the forced buy-back of yen-funded carry positions. There is no configuration in which risk-off is good for this pair. The mitigating consideration, and the reason confidence is only 52, is that the carry-unwind channel is materially less loaded than at any point this cycle: speculative yen positioning has already flipped from 92.2K net short to 72.0K net long and open interest in the yen contract fell 30% in a single week, so the ammunition for a violent squeeze has largely been spent. That lowers the amplitude of a risk-off move without changing its sign. The China channel is the one differentiator with a clean positive sign: Chinese Q2 GDP of 4.3% was the slowest since end-2022, and a stimulus package out of the December Central Economic Work Conference would lift the base leg through iron ore without a matching quote-leg benefit.

Over four weeks a VIX of 16 and tight credit are precisely the conditions in which the widest-carry cross is held. Over six months the starting point is the information: spreads at the floor of their range cannot tighten much and can widen a great deal, and this is the G10 pair with the highest beta to that widening. Confidence is low on both horizons because the credit divergence is the only hard evidence of deterioration and it is one month old.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two legs' speculative positions combine into an amplified rather than a muted pair signal, and the combination is contrarian-positive for AUD/JPY. On the CFTC legacy measure specs are net short 46,814 AUD contracts, having added shorts in each of the three reports into the week the RBA hiked, while specs are net long 72.0K JPY contracts after a 212.6K-contract flip from 92.2K net short — long the quote leg and short the base leg is a crowded short AUD/JPY, and it is the side of the pair that has no fresh buying power left. The yen long sits at roughly the 88th percentile of its own distribution and the 120.4K print of 18 September cleared the 80K threshold both dossiers identify as historically extreme. The composition qualifies the signal in both directions: in the yen, leveraged funds are effectively flat at +7,423 and the long is real money at +41,629 among asset managers, which liquidates slowly rather than gapping; in the Australian dollar, the disaggregated report shows leveraged funds net LONG 58,726, flatly contradicting the legacy short, which is why confidence is 55 and not 70. Engagement has collapsed on both legs — Australian open interest down 37.8% in a week and yen open interest down 30% — so whatever squeeze occurs will be moderate. The structural flow that is unambiguous is Australian: nearly 90% of surveyed superannuation funds expect to raise FX hedge ratios within three months and none expect to cut exposure, which is mechanical AUD buying.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months speculative positioning mean-reverts and institutional flow dominates, and the institutional flows on the two legs are asymmetric in size. On the quote leg, long-dated JGBs now out-yield currency-hedged US Treasuries once 3-4% annual hedge costs are applied, which reverses a two-decade outflow from Japanese life insurers and pension funds running 50-60% hedge ratios against roughly 3.5 trillion dollars of foreign securities; foreign official holdings of US Treasuries falling to a thirty-year low of 13% by July 2026 is the same arithmetic propagating. On the base leg the mirror flow exists and is genuinely AUD-positive — Australian superannuation funds raising hedge ratios generate mechanical AUD buying — but the pools are an order of magnitude apart. The yen-funded carry trade that sits across this pair is estimated at 261bn dollars of direct cross-border borrowing and roughly 1 trillion dollars including derivatives, and its economics have deteriorated to the point where a year's 335bp carry is erased by a 3.4% spot move. Against that, the strategic signal is weak rather than strong: the Australian legacy and disaggregated reports cannot be reconciled, so the level of base-leg exposure is unknown, and the Japanese weekly securities data are not yet confirming a linear repatriation trend, with foreign bond buying at +1,082.9bn yen in the week to 16 September. The 2027-03-31 Japanese fiscal year-end repatriation window falls at the far edge of the horizon and adds a documented seasonal impulse on the same side.

factors.horizon_split: The stances invert because the two horizons read different flows. Over four weeks the operative fact is that specs are short the base and long the quote at a near-extreme, with no buying power left on the short side — a contrarian positive for the pair. Over six months speculative positioning normalises, historically four to eight weeks after an extreme, and what remains is a Japanese institutional reallocation of a multi-trillion-dollar pool against a much smaller Australian hedging flow. The crossover is late October to November, which sits on top of the 30 October BoJ decision.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Amplified rather than muted: specs are net SHORT the base leg (legacy AUD -46,814) and net LONG the quote leg (JPY +72.0K, roughly the 88th percentile), which is a crowded short AUD/JPY with no remaining selling capacity on either side.
tactical.unwind_trigger: Dated and specific: an Australian September quarter trimmed mean at or above 3.7% on 2026-10-28 takes 3 November hike pricing from about 20% through 50%, while a BoJ hold on 2026-10-30 without an Outlook Report forecast upgrade removes the justification for the yen long. The two land two days apart and would force covering on both legs simultaneously.
tactical.historical_analogue: The mirror of July-August 2024, when a leveraged yen SHORT unwound violently and AUD/JPY was the instrument that moved most. This time the leveraged position is on the other side and is far smaller — leveraged funds hold only +7,423 yen contracts against asset managers' +41,629 — so the analogue predicts direction without predicting the violence.
tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is short this pair into two central banks that have both retained an explicit hiking option and that the market prices at a fifth and a third of their stated intent respectively. That is the setup for a squeeze on both legs at once. The case against us is that the shorts are positioned correctly: the RBA may well be finished at 4.60% with unemployment at a post-COVID high and business conditions negative, and the BoJ has told the market it intends to keep going — in which case the crowd is early rather than wrong, and a soft Australian CPI on 28 October vindicates it within the window.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Speculative positioning washes out and the signal becomes the size differential between the two institutional pools: roughly 3.5 trillion dollars of Japanese foreign securities being reconsidered against a far smaller Australian superannuation hedging programme, plus a yen-funded carry book of 261bn to 1 trillion dollars sitting directly across this pair.
strategic.unwind_trigger: An RBA pivot rather than an RBA hike. Australian unemployment through 5.0%, or a trimmed mean back inside the 2-3% band, removes the rationale for holding the widest-carry cross at the same moment the BoJ's Outlook Reports are raising the cost of funding it.
strategic.historical_analogue: The 2007-08 and 2024 carry unwinds, in both of which AUD/JPY led the G10 lower and in both of which the trigger was the funding leg's central bank moving rather than the asset leg's economy failing. The distinguishing feature this cycle is that JGBs finally pay something, which is why the quote leg's institutional flow has a floor it did not have in previous episodes.
strategic.contrarian_case: The contrarian risk to a strategic bearish view is that the carry trade rebuilds faster than the compression arrives. With the differential still 335bp, realised volatility on the cross at 7.82% and VIX at the 28th percentile of its year, the conditions for carry accumulation are present even though the returns recently have not been — a 261bn-to-1-trillion-dollar position has reconstituted itself on exactly this configuration many times before. A December Chinese stimulus package that resets iron ore would supply the missing fundamental justification, and the pair would then be carrying a differential nobody is being paid to fight. Pass-2 addendum (flow evidence from research): the risk is not hypothetical. After the July intervention, long-term investors were reported to be continuing to sell low-yielding yen against higher-yielding G10 currencies, consistent with yen funding positions elsewhere. Meanwhile the Australian-specific bond bid is fading at the margin: Japanese investors were described as having a home-market bias for the first time in many years, with the Australian bond market under pressure from central bank hikes.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the rare pair where the bilateral trade relationship is itself a first-order driver rather than background. IMF Direction of Trade Statistics for 2024 show Australia exporting 46.7bn dollars of goods to Japan against 17.7bn imported, a net Australian surplus of 29.0bn dollars; Japan's own mirror records 52.9bn dollars of imports from Australia against 16.0bn of exports. Japan is Australia's single largest energy customer and the composition of that trade — LNG, thermal and metallurgical coal, iron ore — means the Iran shock transfers real income directly from the quote economy to the base economy. The commodity direction rules all point the same way for this cross: oil up is mildly positive for AUD and strongly negative for JPY, LNG up is strongly negative for JPY, coal up is positive for AUD and negative for JPY, and even iron ore up is positive for AUD and mildly negative for an importing Japan. Current readings are mixed but net favourable: Newcastle coal 145.20 dollars a tonne and +36.72% year-on-year, copper +35.84%, Brent approximately 98 dollars and roughly 50% higher year-on-year, against iron ore at 96.59 dollars and -7.14%. The RBA's own commodity price index was +15.5% year-on-year at the start of September while Japan posted a fourth consecutive monthly goods deficit of 1,105.6bn yen with crude imports up 58.7%. Over four weeks the factor carries only 0.06 of weight and the recent 15% Brent retracement cuts against the signal, which is why confidence is 52.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the external picture splits cleanly into two large forces of similar size pointing in opposite directions, which is what Neutral is for. On the bullish side, the terms-of-trade transfer is structural and has not reversed: Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil and 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East, has run four consecutive goods deficits, and buys most of that energy from the very economy on the other side of this pair. On the bearish side, the aggregate external positions are the mirror image — Japan runs a current account surplus of 5.03% of GDP against Australia's deficit of 3.67%, the third largest in the set, and Australia's own goods and services balance has itself fallen into deficit at 5.1bn Australian dollars with net foreign debt of 1,486.0bn. The valuation gap reinforces the bearish leg and is the most extreme in the entire benchmarking universe: the BIS real effective exchange rate puts the base leg at 116.11, the dearest currency in the set and up 9.97% over a year, against a quote leg at 66.02, the cheapest by 28.8 points and down 6.50 over a year — a 50-point spread between the two legs of a single pair. Australia has achieved that real appreciation while iron ore, 35% of its export revenue, fell 7.14%. Neither side dominates: the income transfer is live and monthly, the valuation gap is extreme but has been extreme for years without mean-reverting, and the Hormuz binary at roughly 25% settlement probability would flip the energy leg abruptly.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Bullish to Neutral as the weight rises from 0.06 to 0.16, because the slow variables only matter when they are given time to work. Over four weeks the operative flow is the monthly energy settlement, which runs one way: Japan buys Australian coal and LNG at prices 37% and more above a year ago. Over six months the cumulative balance-of-payments position and a 50-point real exchange rate gap come into scope and cancel the income transfer. The inflection would be an iron ore recovery above 110 dollars on Chinese stimulus, which is the single change that would make this factor directional again.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Australia: iron ore roughly 35% of export revenue at 96.59 dollars a tonne and -7.14% year-on-year; Newcastle thermal coal 145.20 dollars and +36.72%; LNG a major export to Japan specifically; LME copper +35.84%; a mild net energy exporter in value terms. RBA commodity price index +15.5% year-on-year.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Japan: a pure commodity importer with essentially no offsetting export. Imports approximately 99% of its oil, sources 94.2% of crude from the Middle East, and is one of the world's largest LNG and thermal coal buyers — with Australia as the single largest supplier. Crude imports +58.7% year-on-year, total mineral fuel imports +38.4%, four consecutive monthly goods deficits.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Apply the framework direction rules to each leg and net. Oil up: +AUD (mild, Australia is a modest net energy exporter) and --JPY (strong, 99% import dependence) — net clearly BULLISH AUD/JPY. LNG/JKM up: sometimes +AUD (Australia is a top-two LNG exporter) and --JPY (Japan is the largest LNG importer) — net strongly BULLISH AUD/JPY. Thermal coal up: ++AUD and --JPY — net strongly BULLISH. Iron ore up: ++AUD and mildly negative for an importing Japan — net BULLISH. Copper up: +AUD, mildly negative JPY — net BULLISH. Every component of the complex points the same direction, which is unusual and is what makes this pair the cleanest commodity-exporter-versus-commodity-importer expression in G10. The qualification is that the strength of the rule is contaminated by the risk channel: the same oil spike that transfers income to Australia also triggers the risk-off in which the base leg has the highest beta in G10 and the quote leg is bid, and historically that FX channel dominates the trade channel over one to three months. The net commodity exposure is therefore unambiguously positive in sign and materially weaker in magnitude than the mechanical netting implies.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Mechanically bullish AUD/JPY: Japan's monthly import bill widens directly while Australia's coal and LNG receipts rise, and the base leg's central bank gains justification to extend a cycle the market thinks is over. The offsetting risk channel means the realised impact is well below the mechanical netting, and a move driven by renewed Hormuz disruption rather than demand would likely be net negative for the pair because the global risk-off would dominate.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Mechanically bearish AUD/JPY: Japan's terms of trade improve and its goods deficit narrows, while the base leg loses the supply-side inflation impulse that justifies the highest policy rate in the set. The offset is that a Hormuz settlement is also risk-positive and China-growth-positive, which supports the base leg — so the net fall is smaller than the rule implies and the two effects are close to half-cancelling.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Thermal coal and LNG — the literal content of the 29.0bn dollar bilateral trade surplus. Iron ore is the larger share of total Australian export revenue and matters more for the base leg in isolation, but for THIS pair the energy complex is the direct bilateral transmission, because Japan is the customer.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are guiding hawkish and both are underpriced, which is an unusual and genuinely offsetting configuration. The RBA's 29 September statement was unanimous, judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted and retained the option explicitly, with Bullock stating the Board will increase rates again if needed and calling the fuel shock permanently higher; the market prices 3 November at roughly 20%. The BoJ's 18 September statement guided that it will continue raising the policy rate, and the Summary of Opinions published 30 September has a majority favouring further hikes with one member arguing to accelerate; the market prices 30 October at 25-38%. The probability gap is larger on the base leg — roughly 25 points against roughly 10 — but the event asymmetry runs the other way: the gated calendar marks the BoJ's 30 October meeting as carrying an Outlook Report, a projection round that moves a pair materially harder than a bare statement, while it carries no projection note for the RBA on 3 November. Sequencing compounds it: the BoJ decides four days before the RBA, so it sets the tone and the base leg cannot respond inside the same week. Multiplying probability gap by expected spot impact leaves the two almost exactly offsetting, which is why this is Neutral at 50 rather than a directional call in either direction.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the asymmetry in how much each bank has left to deliver, and how much each has to lose by reversing, tilts the pair lower. The gated calendar gives the BoJ three decisions inside the window with two Outlook Report projection rounds, on 30 October and 22 January, against the RBA's two bare decisions on 3 November and 8 December. A central bank that signals through forecast revisions and holds two forecast rounds has more scheduled opportunity to raise the market's terminal-rate estimate than one with none. Credibility cuts the other way on each leg: the RBA has delivered four hikes in 2026 and is maximally credible today, but it has told the market it will keep going while its own unemployment rate hits a post-COVID high of 4.6% and business conditions turn negative, so it has the most to reverse; the BoJ is the least transparent communicator in G10 and its two most consequential shifts both surprised markets, but it has now delivered two hikes in 2026 against an expansionary Takaichi administration widely assumed to prefer accommodation, which is the strongest available evidence on independence. A third element belongs here and has no base-leg equivalent: the Ministry of Finance and the US Treasury have jointly confirmed the late-July coordinated intervention and both have signalled readiness to repeat it, which is forward guidance on the exchange rate itself and caps the pair's upside without capping its downside. Confidence is only 45 because both banks are hawkish and the differential in guidance quality is a matter of degree.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bearish because the tactical case is a single pair of underpriced binaries that offset, while the strategic case is a cadence difference that compounds: two projection rounds against none, three decisions against two, and a base-leg central bank whose stated reaction function has to survive a deteriorating labour market for six months. Confidence is lower strategically at 45 because both banks are hawkish and the edge is in degree rather than direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The dominant event is the Strait of Hormuz and for this pair specifically it is close to two-sided, because each outcome hits the two legs through different channels that partly cancel. Escalation raises Brent, which transfers income from the quote economy to the base economy through the bilateral energy trade, but simultaneously triggers the risk-off in which the base leg has the highest beta in G10 and the quote leg is the standard haven — historically the FX channel dominates the trade channel over one to three months, so escalation is net bearish for the pair despite the terms-of-trade logic. De-escalation reverses both signs and is net ambiguous: risk-on and a China growth impulse lift the base leg while the removal of the base-leg central bank's hiking rationale and the relief to Japan's import bill lift the quote leg. Export volumes have recovered to 16.328 million barrels a day, roughly 80% of pre-war, Iran proposed reopening within seven days in exchange for sanctions relief, Trump rejected it, and UN General Assembly talks were described as productive with the disagreement over sequencing. That is a live near-dated binary with no clean sign for this cross. The intervention put is not binding at current levels — the trigger is a revisit of the pre-intervention zone on the quote leg's dollar pair, which is some distance away — so it does not truncate the tactical distribution. Australian domestic political risk is negligible with no federal election due until May 2028.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the event set widens and the balance tips against the pair, because the yen-positive tails are more numerous than the AUD-positive ones and the pair's beta to each is higher. Three events carry a quote-leg-positive sign: a second coordinated US-Japan intervention, assessed at roughly 20% conditional on a revisit of the pre-intervention zone, which would produce a gap rather than a drift and would hit AUD/JPY harder than any other cross because broad yen strength lands fully on the widest-carry pair; a Hormuz re-escalation at roughly 15%, in which the risk-off channel dominates the terms-of-trade channel for this specific cross; and any China-Taiwan deterioration, a low-probability tail that is unambiguously bad for the base leg and good for the quote leg. One event carries a clean base-leg-positive sign and it is the most probable single item: the Chinese Central Economic Work Conference in December and the National People's Congress in March, with Chinese Q2 GDP at 4.3% — the slowest since end-2022 — against first-half exports up 17.6%, the widest domestic-demand gap of the cycle and the strongest case for a property or infrastructure package in years. That transmits through iron ore, 35% of base-leg export revenue, and is assessed at roughly 20%. One is quote-leg-negative: the Japanese FY2027 budget in December with Fitch publicly committed to scrutinising it. The net is a modest bearish tilt rather than a dominant one, which is why confidence is 50.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bearish because the composition of the event set changes with the window rather than its centre. Over four weeks the Hormuz binary is the only live item and its two channels cancel for this pair. Over six months the intervention put, a re-escalation tail and a China-Taiwan tail all carry the same quote-leg-positive sign and are only partly offset by the single clean base-leg-positive event, Chinese stimulus. Confidence is low on both horizons because the offsets are genuine.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The sovereign differential between these two legs is the widest in the benchmarking set and it is not currently material over four weeks. Australia holds Aaa from Moody's and AAA from S&P and Fitch, all stable, with net general government debt at 18.8% of GDP and an underlying cash deficit of 1.6% of GDP; Japan carries A1, A+ and A with a debt stock near 260% of GDP, the heaviest in the developed world. That is a four-to-five notch rating gap and a debt ratio more than thirteen times larger. Neither fact moves the pair inside a month: there is no rating review, auction failure or supply event scheduled on either side, Japanese auctions are clearing with the late-September 40-year sale drawing the strongest demand since 2020 and the 30 September two-year clearing at 1.964%, and Japanese yields actually fell across the curve on 30 September on a report that the Prime Minister would pledge a swift response to market developments. The transmission mechanism that would make this factor live — a long-end repricing read as sovereign risk rather than normalisation — requires a catalyst and none is scheduled inside the window. The relative-value observation worth recording is that the quote leg's 30-year at 4.15% against a 2-year at 1.93% is a 222bp curve that increasingly reflects term premium rather than policy, which is the configuration in which rising yields would start to weaken rather than strengthen the quote currency.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices an immaterial fiscal premium at the front of both curves and an increasingly material one at the Japanese long end. Over four weeks there is no mechanism by which either prices into the cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months fiscal quality becomes a genuine differentiator for this pair and it is the one factor that points the pair higher. The base leg has more fiscal space than any economy in the benchmarking set — 18.8% net debt, a 1.6%-of-GDP deficit, triple-A from all three agencies with stable outlooks and a projected net debt path of 19.9%, 21.0% and 21.8% that stays below the 28.3% peak of 2020 — which means it has the greatest capacity to cushion the slowdown its own central bank is engineering. The quote leg is running the opposite experiment: an expansionary administration including a food tax cut, a debt stock near 260% of GDP, a 10-year that has risen 141bp in a year and a 30-year at 4.15%, with each 100bp on the average yield eventually costing roughly 2% of GDP in debt service as it passes through the stock. The dated catalyst sits inside the window: the FY2027 budget is compiled in December and Fitch has publicly committed to reviewing it for the balance between growth and fiscal discipline. The transmission is the one that is usually missed — higher JGB yields are quote-leg-positive through the differential channel but quote-leg-negative through the sovereign-risk channel, and which dominates depends on whether the rise is normalisation or term premium. A 222bp 2s30s says the market is increasingly pricing the latter. Confidence is 58 rather than higher because Japanese ratings are stable, auctions clear, and 90% domestic ownership remains the shock absorber it has always been.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bullish because fiscal quality has no tactical trigger and a dated strategic one. Inside four weeks auctions clear on both sides, ratings are stable and nothing is scheduled. Inside six months the Japanese FY2027 budget lands in December with Fitch watching, three BoJ decisions each add to the debt-service arithmetic, and the base leg's 18.8% net debt ratio determines how much counter-cyclical room it has as its own tightening bites. tactical.rationale: At the applied tactical weights the pair is decided by Policy and Rates at 0.27, Inflation and Growth at 0.15 and Risk Appetite at 0.14, which together carry 56% of the score, and the heaviest of the three resolves Neutral. That matters: the 335bp policy differential is the widest in the G10+SGD set and the single largest fundamental support under the cross, but its level is cancelled over four weeks by two central banks that have each retained an explicit hiking option the market prices at roughly a fifth and a third of its stated intent. The RBA's 29 September unanimous hike to 4.60% and the BoJ's 18 September 7-2 hike to 1.25% both came with guidance to continue, and both legs therefore carry an underpriced hawkish binary inside the same fortnight. The two standalone dossiers interact constructively rather than conflicting: the base currency is tactically Bullish at +0.304 on an underpriced 3 November RBA hike, and the quote currency is tactically Neutral at -0.028 with a marginal yen-BEARISH tilt, so the combination points the cross higher without either leg driving it hard. The bilateral factors that modify those standalone views are the ones that make this pair different from the sum of its parts. First, positioning combines rather than muting: specs are net short 46,814 contracts of the base leg on the legacy measure and net long 72.0K contracts of the quote leg at roughly the 88th percentile, which is an amplified crowded SHORT AUD/JPY with no fresh selling capacity left on either side. Second, the bilateral trade relationship is first-order and runs one way: IMF DOTS records a 29.0bn dollar Australian goods surplus with Japan, overwhelmingly energy, so an oil complex roughly 50% higher year-on-year and coal 36.72% higher transfers real income directly from the quote economy to the base economy every month. Third, this is the purest risk-beta pair in G10, and with VIX at the 28th percentile of its year and equities up 14% the regime level supports it even as high yield widening 42bp warns at the margin. What is priced is an RBA that has finished, a BoJ that moves slowly, and a benign risk tape; what we expect is an Australian September quarter trimmed mean on 28 October at or above 3.6% that forces 3 November repricing while the quote leg's own hawkish surprise is smaller in probability if larger in impact. The path of least resistance is therefore a grind higher into the 28 October to 3 November cluster, driven as much by short-covering as by new conviction. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the thesis is one datapoint wide — a soft Australian trimmed mean removes the largest of four weak legs in a single print — because the base leg's own positioning evidence is internally contradictory, with a disaggregated leveraged-fund net long of 58,726 flatly contradicting the legacy short, and because a long position that is paid 352bp a year on the roll is a pleasant thing to hold but not a reason to hold it. Pass-2 view on the tactical call: we publish the tactical Bullish as issued, but we think it is the weaker of the two calls. The price structure is a falling one. The September close percentile slid into the low 70s from the 90s. And the main datable pillar, a hawkish repricing of 3 November, was already weakening in commentary published after the spot date. Size the call accordingly.

The largest weight on the board after Factor 1 — External Balance at 0.16 — scores zero, and that zero is substantive rather than lazy: a 29.0bn dollar bilateral energy surplus flowing from the quote economy to the base economy is squarely offset by an 870bp current-account gap and a 50-point BIS real exchange rate gap running the other way. strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the pair is decided by Policy and Rates at 0.27, External Balance at 0.16, Guidance at 0.12 and Risk Appetite plus USD Liquidity at 0.08 each — 71% of the weight in five blocks — and only one of the five supports the pair. The dominant mechanism is not the level of the 335bp differential but its direction of travel. The gated calendar gives the BoJ three decisions inside the window with two Outlook Report projection rounds on 30 October and 22 January, against two bare RBA decisions on 3 November and 8 December: the quote leg's central bank has more remaining tightening than any peer and two scheduled vehicles for raising the market's terminal-rate estimate, while the base leg's central bank sits 60bp above the top of its band with unemployment at a post-COVID 4.6%, NAB business conditions negative for the first time since September 2020 and sales margins at -20. Two BoJ hikes against at most one RBA hike takes the gap toward 285-310bp, and the terminal repricing is worth more than the steps. The two standalone dossiers conflict in exactly the way that produces this score: the base currency is strategically Neutral at +0.031, held back by a 3.67%-of-GDP current account deficit and a real exchange rate at 116.11 that is both the dearest level and the largest one-year appreciation in the set, while the quote currency is strategically Bullish at +0.250 on a REER of 66.02 that is 28.8 points below the next-cheapest currency. A 50-point real exchange rate gap between the two legs of one pair is the most extreme valuation divergence in the benchmarking universe, and it is why the external-balance factor nets to zero rather than supporting the pair despite a genuine bilateral energy income transfer. Bilateral specifics modify the standalone views in three ways. First, this is the maximum-beta risk pair in G10, so credit at the floor of its post-crisis range is a double-sided liability here that it is not elsewhere. Second, the coordinated US-Japan intervention commitment caps the pair's upside and nothing caps its downside — a one-sided official put that lands fully on the widest-carry cross. Third, the hedged-yield crossover reallocating a 3.5 trillion dollar Japanese pool has no base-leg equivalent of comparable size. What is priced is the full 335bp carry in the forwards and essentially nothing of the compression; what we expect is that the compression arrives through the two Outlook Reports while the base leg's cycle ends. The path of least resistance is a stepped drift lower keyed to the scheduled BoJ decisions rather than a trend, with the December Chinese Central Economic Work Conference as the single clean interruption. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because a short pays 352bp a year to be held, because the one clean upside catalyst — a Chinese stimulus package that resets iron ore — is the most probable single event in the strategic set at roughly 20%, and because the 50-point valuation gap has been wide for years without mean-reverting and is a reason rather than a timer. Pass-2 view on the strategic call: the price payload supports this call. The April–August 111–115 range has broken to the downside, and the 50-day has crossed below the 100-day. The absence of any computed support between 108.74 and 101.04 means a fall, once under way, has little in its path. We agree with the direction and judge the main risk to be carry cost and timing rather than structure.

risk_reward.expected_value: Pair move: 0.50 x (-481) + 0.25 x (+369) + 0.25 x (-831) = -356 pips, i.e. +356 pips to a short gross. Net of about 193 pips of six-month carry the short earns about +163 pips. Carry-adjusted from spot the base case nets +288 and the upside case -562, which is why the trade should not be initiated at spot.
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: Favourable once entered on a rebound: the intervention put caps the pair's upside, while below 108.74 there is no computed support for 876 pips. Preferred construction: sell 111.00–111.45 (former range floor, 200-day) after the 28 October – 3 November cluster; stop 112.70 (above the 100-day at 112.61 and the 18 September high, about 1.6x ATR); target 1 is 108.00 and target 2 is 105.00. From a 111.20 entry the base case pays 620 pips against 150 pips of stop risk (4.1:1). Size a full standard unit for conviction 3 on the 150-pip stop (0.75–1.0% capital at risk); options-based downside exposure is the alternative for those who cannot fund a six-month carry bleed, although the skew makes AUD puts on this cross rich.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bullish, conviction 2, net weighted score +0.1978. The pair rises over two to four weeks on a widening inflation differential, a supportive risk level, a crowded short position on the cross and a one-way bilateral energy income transfer, against a firm dollar.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish, conviction 3, net weighted score -0.3413. The pair falls over one to six months as a 335bp differential compresses toward 285-310bp through two BoJ Outlook Reports against at most one RBA hike, while the inflation gap narrows from both ends and the risk and funding asymmetries both run against the cross.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Tactically ABOVE the triangulated consensus path (which implies the fall begins immediately); strategically IN LINE with the direction of the six-month triangulation and LESS bearish than the Q1-2027 triangulation implies; below the pair-specific (non-bank) aggregate forecast on the strategic horizon.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Versus the pair-specific aggregate (updated 20 September; 112.15 by December 2026, 113.12 by March 2027): one month, our expected spot is 110.50 against 112.24, 174 pips lower; six months, our probability-weighted expected spot is 106.25 against 113.12, 687 pips lower. Versus the pass-1 cross-implied triangulation (roughly 109.2-112.2 at six months, 104.7-107.6 by Q1 2027), our 106.25 sits inside the Q1-2027 range. The forward curve already prepays part of the strategic move: the roll is -351.9bp annualised, roughly -1.76% over six months.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: No bank research forecast for AUD/JPY specifically could be sourced, and none is asserted; the pass-1 triangulation (base-leg USD consensus 0.72-0.74 at three to twelve months times a quote-leg aggregator forecast of 151.62 at six months and 145.40 by Q1 2027) implies a derived 109.2-112.2 at six months and 104.7-107.6 by Q1 2027, inheriting two layers of source uncertainty. The disagreement with that triangulation is about path, not direction: it has the pair falling from the start, whereas we think the fall starts later and stops sooner. Later, because specs are net short 46,814 contracts of the base leg and net long 72.0K of the quote leg at roughly the 88th percentile, so the crowded trade is already the short, the yen squeeze fuel has been consumed by a 212.6K-contract flip, and both legs carry an underpriced hawkish central bank inside the same fortnight. Sooner, because consensus underweights the 29.0bn dollar bilateral goods surplus Australia runs with Japan (overwhelmingly energy, Brent roughly 50% above a year ago) and a four-to-five notch sovereign differential that meets a Japanese FY2027 budget in December under a committed Fitch review. Against the pair-specific aggregate (a retail algorithmic-style extrapolation, not bank research) we differ because it appears to extrapolate the carry and weight neither the BoJ's two projection rounds nor the institutional repatriation channel; its path is flat-to-higher for six months while ours is a squeeze followed by a stepped decline. The two reference points disagree with each other by 6–8 yen, itself evidence that nobody has a confident view on the funding leg. Where we agree with consensus, and where the edge is thinnest, is on the direction of the policy differential itself.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the tactical call is right, the pair rises into the 28 October to 3 November cluster while a rolled long is simultaneously paid roughly 352bp a year, so carry and direction compound rather than offset. If the strategic call is right, the differential compression and the institutional reallocation deliver a fall that the forward curve has only partly prepaid; a short from 111.20 earns 620 pips to 105.00 against a consensus that implies holding the carry, and the cleanest expression avoids paying the full carry to wait.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: On the tactical call, a soft Australian September quarter trimmed mean on 28 October removes the largest of four individually weak bullish legs in a single print and the crowded short is vindicated rather than squeezed. On the strategic call, the loss case is a Chinese stimulus package out of the December Central Economic Work Conference that resets iron ore above 115 dollars while the RBA is still hiking and the BoJ stalls at 1.25% under political pressure; if the aggregate is right the pair grinds back to 113 and the short is stopped at 112.70, a defined 150-pip loss, and a short pays 352bp a year to be wrong.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge by 0.539 points and the divergence is mechanical rather than contradictory. The same 335bp differential drives both: its LEVEL binds over four weeks, where it is the widest carry in the set and two underpriced hawkish central banks cancel each other out, and its TRAJECTORY binds over one to six months, where the BoJ has three decisions and two projection rounds against the RBA's two bare decisions. Three factors flip sign across the horizons and each flip has a stated mechanism. Flows and Positioning is Bullish tactically because specs are crowded short the cross with no selling capacity left, and Bearish strategically because speculative positioning normalises in four to eight weeks and leaves a 3.5 trillion dollar Japanese institutional reallocation as the signal. Inflation and Growth is Bullish tactically because a widening gap means a higher probability of an Australian hike, and Bearish strategically because the same energy shock compressing Australian margins is building an unpassed 5.7-point Japanese price pipeline. Risk Appetite is Bullish tactically on the level of a benign tape and Bearish strategically on the asymmetry from credit at the floor of its post-crisis range.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 30 October BoJ decision with Outlook Report, followed by the 3 November RBA decision four days later, with the Australian September quarter CPI on 28 October as the trigger. That three-event cluster is where the tactical positioning thesis resolves and where the strategic compression thesis either begins or is deferred to 18 December. The secondary inflection is the normalisation of speculative yen positioning below roughly +30K contracts, historically four to eight weeks after an extreme, which places it in late October or November.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The two views are compatible if sequenced and incompatible if held simultaneously. The tactical long is a short-duration, catalyst-dependent position that is paid to wait and that should not be carried through the 30 October to 3 November cluster unresolved; the strategic short pays roughly 352bp a year to be held and therefore needs either a dated catalyst, an options expression, or entry after the October cluster has repriced the positioning liability out of the cross. Holding the tactical view past the inflection converts a positive-carry directional trade into a negative-carry one against a thesis that has already changed sign. Pass-2 level mapping: the two views hand over at the same place on the chart. The tactical long's target band of 111.00–111.43 is the strategic short's entry band; if the squeeze delivers, take profit on the long and sell into the same zone. If the pair closes below 108.40 before the cluster, the long is stopped, and the short is better added on a retest of 108.74–109.24 (the broken October and August lows), because the carry cost no longer justifies waiting for 111.

catalysts.event: BoJ Governor Ueda speech; Japan August labour cash earnings

A fifth consecutive goods deficit would confirm the energy income transfer that supports the pair. A strong primary-income headline is largely reinvested abroad and does not buy yen.

Unemployment at 4.6% is the main obstacle to a 3 November hike. A print of 4.7% or higher both weakens the tactical case and begins the strategic pivot. A fall to 4.5% with full-time gains strengthens the squeeze.

The trigger for the tactical thesis. Trimmed mean of 3.7% or higher takes November pricing above 50% and forces covering in a cross that is crowded short on both legs. The softer post-spot monthly indicators raise the bar.
Works through the dollar smile and the hedge-cost path. A hike keeps the dollar firm (mildly negative for the cross); a hold supports the base leg's risk beta. Roughly 30% is priced in.

The highest-stakes event of the quarter for this pair. A hike or a forecast upgrade compresses the differential four days before the RBA can respond, and would end the tactical long. Hike probability priced at roughly 25–38%.
The resolution point and hard exit date for the tactical long. A hike against roughly 20% pricing produces the upside scenario. A hold with dovish language opens the strategic short.

Decides whether 5.0% Australian unemployment arrives inside the window. A print of 4.8% or higher raises strategic conviction (the ladder moves to 4), while a softer print supports the tactical long and the case that the RBA is not yet finished.

catalysts.rationale: The first test of whether the 7.6% producer-price pipeline passes through to consumer prices. It closes the 190bp core gap from the Japanese side and gives the BoJ cover to keep hiking, compressing the differential that supports the pair.

Fixes the market's estimate of the base leg's terminal rate, the numerator of the whole carry case. A hike to 4.85% would widen the differential toward 360bp, while a hold with dovish language supports the strategic compression thesis.

catalysts.event: China Central Economic Work Conference — week 2 of December, exact date approximate
catalysts.rationale: The single clean pair-positive strategic event, transmitting through iron ore (35% of Australian export revenue) with no matching quote-leg benefit. It is the specific way the strategic short loses money, assessed at roughly 20% probability of major stimulus.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 budget and Fitch review window — week 3 of December, exact date approximate
catalysts.rationale: A disappointing budget reprices the JGB long end as term premium, which weakens the yen and lifts the pair. It is the dated mechanism behind the only positive strategic factor.

The second hike opportunity, priced at roughly 39%. It becomes the focal point if 30 October holds with a hawkish revision, and a hike here would deliver the first step of the strategic differential compression.
The second projection round. It confirms or invalidates the compression thesis and sets up the March fiscal-year-end repatriation window, the last scheduled impulse inside the strategic horizon.

The spotDate of 2026-10-02 is one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date and anchors every level, pip calculation, percentage and moving-average distance; no web-quoted spot was substituted. The resistance shortfall is handled with round numbers (111.00, 112.00, 115.00), the 50/100/200-day averages and the 52-week high, each labelled supplementary.
Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Zone distances are measured to the band midpoint, matching the payload distancePips field; edge distances are stated where they matter.

Realised volatility (6.79% 20-day, 7.87% 60-day) and ATR(14) (93 pips) come from the payload. Implied volatility is the store's triangulated estimate (7.925 / 7.702 / 7.827% at 36.7 / 99.7 / 190.6 days), carried as a floor with its documented 14.4% median understatement. No IV percentile or pair risk reversal is observable.

Forward outrights are derived from the −351.9bp CME calendar-spread roll premium using simple interest, and are not dealer-quoted points. 10-year yields in the payload are monthly vintages as of 2026-08-01 and are not live levels.

Factor scores, stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, contributions, net scores (+0.1978 tactical, −0.3413 strategic), convictions, score interpretations, rationales, G10 rankings, the pass-1 consensus text and the cross-horizon text are carried verbatim from the pass-1 Direction Verdict. Three inconsistencies are noted but not corrected: pass 1 quotes 60-day realised volatility of 7.82% (dossier) where the payload gives 7.87%; its one-month breakeven of 0.84% conflicts with its own 0.28%-a-month accrual (this report uses 0.28%, 31 pips); and its factor citations refer to the pass-1 reference list.

Scenario levels, probabilities, entries, stops, sizing and expected values are pass-2 judgements anchored to the payload. Carry is netted separately at 3.35% annualised (about 28 pips per four weeks, about 193 pips per six months on the roll). The tactical horizon runs to 2026-11-03; the strategic horizon runs to end-March 2027.

Six bilateral web searches were run (forecasts, technicals, positioning and carry, Japanese investment in Australian bonds, options). Several results are dated after the spotDate (5–6 October 2026) and are used only as commentary and signposts, never as price inputs. One pair-specific consensus aggregate (four providers, updated 20 September) is reported as a separate input. No pair-specific bank research, quoted risk reversals or AUD/JPY cross-currency basis could be sourced; these are documented gaps. Bilateral trade uses the supplied IMF DOTS 2024 block (Australian goods surplus with Japan US$29.0bn) without re-estimation.

Formatter notes: (a) annualised_carry_bps is recorded as +351.9 (a long earns), the sign convention required by the schema; the source report labels the same roll premium as −351.9bp in forward-point terms (AUD at a forward discount).
